task:

Data: the file `forcing.csv` in your working folder holds daily data from 1970-10-01 to 1997-12-31 with the columns
Date (format YYYYMMDD), Precipitation (mm/day), Temperature (degrees C), PotentialET (mm/day) and Discharge (observed
streamflow, mm/day, with gaps marked as missing values). Treat 1970-10-01 to 1971-09-30 as model warm-up.

Goal: find the parameter set that will simulate daily streamflow best in a later, independent period (1998 to 2008)
that you do not have. Your submission will be scored only by the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of daily streamflow
in that period.

Budget: at most 50 tool calls (submit_calibration does not count) and 10000 model runs. Every
simulation of the period is one model run, including each run inside calibrate and evaluate_uncertainty. The budget
left is reported after each tool call.

To finish, call submit_calibration with the model_id of your final model and a short diagnosis (at most 200 words):
how well the model performs, which processes or periods it simulates poorly, and how confident you are in the
parameters. A run that ends without submit_calibration counts as a failure.

definitions.name: create_model
definitions.description:
Create a new HBV model instance and return its model_id.

    All other tools operate on a model referenced by this id.

definitions.name: list_models
definitions.description: List the model_ids currently held in the server registry.

definitions.name: load_data
definitions.description:
Load forcing data into a model from a CSV or Excel (.xlsx) file on disk.

    Pass the column names used in the file. ``obs_q_column`` (observed discharge) is
    optional but required for calibration, uncertainty analysis and performance
    metrics. Dates use ``date_format`` (e.g. '%Y%m%d' for 19810101). ``warmup_end`` /
    ``start_date`` / ``end_date`` are optional date filters (same format).

    Potential ET may be given as a full daily series OR as exactly 12 values (monthly
    means, the HBV-light convention) — in the latter case it is **expanded to a daily
    series automatically**. The return reports ``pet_handling`` so you know which path
    was taken, plus a ``data_quality`` summary (valid/missing counts and min/max per
    column) so you don't have to open the file to sanity-check the inputs.

definitions.name: get_parameters
definitions.description:
Return the model's current parameter values (the 'default' of each), grouped,
    plus an ``at_bound`` list flagging any parameter pinned to its min/max range.

definitions.name: get_parameter_ranges
definitions.description:
Return the min / max / default of every parameter (the ranges the optimizer and
    Monte-Carlo uncertainty sampling use), grouped.

definitions.name: set_parameter_ranges
definitions.description:
Widen or narrow parameter search ranges from a flat mapping, e.g.
    {"FC": {"min": 50, "max": 500}, "CFMAX": {"max": 10}}.

    Each entry may set any of "min" / "max" / "default"; the group is resolved
    automatically. Use this when calibrate reports a parameter ``at_bound`` — widen its
    range, then calibrate again. Unknown names are reported and ignored.

definitions.name: set_parameters
definitions.description:
Set parameter values from a flat mapping, e.g. {"FC": 250, "MAXBAS": 4}.

    Each named parameter's 'default' is updated; its group (snow/soil/response) is
    resolved automatically. Unknown names are reported and ignored.

definitions.name: set_initial_conditions
definitions.description:
Set the initial storage of each model store (mm) at the start of the loaded period.

    Omitted states keep their current value. The defaults are snowpack 0, liquid_water 0,
    soil_moisture 30, upper_storage 10 and lower_storage 20 mm. Every run, calibration and
    uncertainty run starts from these values, and clone_model copies them (copy_parameters
    does not).

    When it matters: a store that starts far from its usual level drifts during the first
    part of the run. A warm-up period hides a short drift, but slow stores (a large FC, or
    a small K2 in groundwater-fed catchments) can take years to settle, longer than the
    warm-up. run_model reports each store's level at the start, its mean and its level at
    the end of the run (``stores``). If a store ends far from where it started, setting its
    initial value near its mean or end level gives a run that starts close to equilibrium.

definitions.name: run_model
definitions.description:
Run the simulation over the loaded period. Returns a compact summary +
    performance metrics (if observed discharge was provided).

    ``stores`` gives each store's level (mm) at the start, its mean over the run and its
    level at the end. A large difference between start and end means the store had not
    reached equilibrium at the start (see set_initial_conditions).

definitions.name: calibrate
definitions.description:
Calibrate the model to observed discharge (requires obs data loaded).

    ``objective`` is one of NSE / KGE / RMSE / MAE. ``method`` is a gradient-free
    optimiser: 'Nelder-Mead' (default, local), 'Powell' (local) or 'DDS'
    (Dynamically Dimensioned Search, global, designed for hydrological model
    calibration). For 'DDS', ``iterations`` is the number of model runs
    (about 1000 to 5000 is typical) and ``seed`` makes the run repeatable.

    Progress: while running, the server emits MCP progress notifications each
    optimizer iteration (visible in clients that surface them).

    Incremental use: each call continues from the model's *current* parameters, so an
    agent can call calibrate repeatedly with a small ``iterations`` budget (e.g. 50),
    inspect the improving metric and ``objective_trajectory`` between calls, and decide
    whether to keep going, widen parameter ranges, or switch objective.

    Returns the optimized parameters, final metrics, optimizer status, and the
    best-objective-per-iteration trajectory (downsampled).

definitions.name: evaluate_uncertainty
definitions.description:
Monte-Carlo uncertainty analysis (requires obs data loaded).

    Samples the parameter ranges ``n_runs`` times and keeps the ``save_best`` runs, then
    forms a 95% prediction band from them. Returns diagnostics: the 95% band
    ``coverage`` (fraction of observations inside the band), ``mean_band_width``, and the
    per-parameter posterior **quantiles** (p5/p25/p50/p75/p95) across the best sets.

    If ``output_file`` is given, the full **per-timestep prediction band** is written to
    that CSV (Date, Observed, Calibrated, BestRun, Q5, Q95) — this is the band itself,
    ready to plot. Sampling is uniform over the parameter ranges (this is parameter, not
    predictive, uncertainty).

definitions.name: clone_model
definitions.description:
Deep-copy a model (parameters, data, states, results) into a new model_id.

    The canonical split-sample pattern: calibrate ``model-A``, ``clone_model`` it, then
    ``load_data`` the validation window on the clone and ``run_model`` — the calibrated
    parameters carry over, no manual parameter transfer needed.

definitions.name: copy_parameters
definitions.description:
Copy the calibrated parameters (and ranges) from one model to another.

    Use this to transfer a calibration to a validation model without copying its data.

definitions.name: get_metrics
definitions.description:
Return the model's current performance metrics without re-running it.

    Empty if the model hasn't been run with observed discharge yet.

definitions.name: compare_models
definitions.description:
Tabulate performance metrics across several models side by side.

    Handy for comparing calibration vs validation, or several calibration variants.

definitions.name: submit_calibration
definitions.description:
Submit your final calibrated model. This ends the task.

    ``model_id`` is the model whose current parameters are your answer. ``diagnosis`` is a short text (at most about
    200 words): how well the model performs, which processes or periods it simulates poorly, and how confident you
    are in the parameters. Only the first submission counts.

message.thinking:
The NSE is -0.25, which is quite bad. The observed flow peaks at 1.57 mm/day, so the mean is probably around 0.4 mm/day, which suggests the catchment loses a lot of water. With precipitation at 2.08 and PET at 1.38, actual ET can't be much above 1.2, which leaves roughly 0.9 mm/day. That still doesn't match the observed mean, so the model is losing less water than it should.

The model's PBIAS is still 17%, and the correlation of only 0.376 is weak. Chalk groundwater has long memory, so with K2 this small the lower storage barely moves, which looks odd. The observed record might also carry trends from upstream effluent, though I'm not certain of the sewage works' position. Next I'll run the model and check the stores and mean flows, since a growing lower storage would make the future-period results meaningless.

I'm checking the observed discharge, about 0.125 mm/day with a runoff ratio of 0.06, against the Wandle's mean flow at Connollys Mill.

The soil store finished near 931 after years of filling, and the lower storage keeps climbing toward 3649, so the model is acting as a large sink. With baseflow K2 times lower storage already around 0.27, the outflow term keeps rising, which is a problem for any future simulation. I need a version that removes roughly 94% of precipitation, and since even full evapotranspiration at potential rates leaves far more water than the observed 0.125 mm/day, the snow and temperature settings will have to do much of that work.

I'm weighing whether the future run would even start from the default lower-storage value, since that's unknown and makes the current sink behavior risky. Setting K2 to its lower bound would make the lower store a pure sink with negligible outflow, so the flow would come only from the upper storage, with PERC as a constant loss that could remove most of the precipitation. Still, the observed baseflow is strongly seasonal, and a constant-rate loss might not reproduce that.

I'm considering that the observed correlation is so low, maybe because the data is affected by abstraction and augmentation, which would make it hard to calibrate. I'd rather keep the temperature threshold reasonable and try a fixed tiny K2 with wider parameter ranges, though using snow as a precipitation sink adds timing problems since melt gets delayed.

I'm going to try a configuration with K2 pinned near zero, so the lower store acts as a pure sink and the upper store's PERC loss does most of the removal. I'll also run a version with the snow and temperature settings restricted, then compare the fits.

I'm setting the upper zone's quick-flow and drainage rates to work as a two-component model with a loss term, and I'm widening the K1 lower bound to 0.001 before running it.

The current parameters fall outside the new ranges, so I'll reset them to defaults: TT 0, SFCF 1, K2 1e-6. I also want to set the initial soil moisture, maybe around 150, but since FC is variable I'll start it at 100 instead.

message.thinking: The fit is now at NSE 0.22, a bit better. The slow store's timescale is about 430 days, and the upper store looks large and sluggish. Bias sits at -22%, so I'm wondering whether the observations carry a long-term upward trend, and I'll run it and check the stores.

I'm noticing soil moisture starts at 150 and averages around 1543, so the soil is still filling during the first many years and that spin-up is skewing the early results. I think the model is effectively using soil as a sink at the start, which means it isn't stationary yet. Setting the initial soil near equilibrium around 1550 looks like the fix, but that equilibrium depends on field capacity, so I'm weighing how large that capacity value is.

I'm working through the soil moisture numbers: with 1543 against a field capacity of 2829, evapotranspiration and recharge both come out to roughly two-thirds of potential ET and about half of precipitation. The real problem looks like the large storage acting as a sink, with percolation draining the upper zone well beyond what the observed flow supports. I'm also weighing how the scoring run starts, since a large field capacity with slow spin-up could badly distort results if the evaluation uses default initial states.

I'm weighing whether the evaluator starts from default soil states or from the model's own initial conditions, since a field capacity this large could stall flow entirely if the run begins dry. A smaller capacity would equilibrate within about a year, which would be more robust. I'm also considering whether the upper zone should act as the groundwater store and the lower zone as the sink, since the dead store is the only available loss beyond evapotranspiration.

I'm narrowing the field capacity range to around 50 to 500, since the large value was stalling flow, and I'm raising the upper zone threshold so quick responses can register. I'll start the initial soil moisture near 200 and run the DDS calibration from there.

I'm setting the DDS calibration to run for 1500 iterations.

The model is doing worse now, with a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency below zero and a PBIAS of about -40%. The observed hydrograph seems to carry something the model can't reproduce, possibly multi-year baseflow variability from the chalk, since the Wandle's flows track groundwater levels that integrate winter recharge over years. The earlier run with the large field capacity captured part of that, so I'm considering a lower storage setting as an alternative.

I'm weighing whether a lower storage setting could stand in for the missing sink, but the only real loss in this model is evapotranspiration, which doesn't cover it. Working through the water balance, recharge still looks far too high against the observed flow, so some extra sink is needed regardless.

I'm considering whether the model's lower store, with its tiny outflow constant, might be producing a slow rising trend in flow. The first model's storage grew a lot over the run, while the second's barely contributed. Neither result is convincing yet, since the first one still has a negative NSE.

I'm wondering whether the observed flows include something like a trend from the early years, since the second model only reaches a reasonable fit because its soil starts out dry and suppresses flow in the first few years. If the evaluation period starts from the same initial conditions with no warm-up, that spin-up effect could distort the results.

I'm checking whether the early-period spin-up is what made the second model fit, so I'm going to rerun it with the soil starting at equilibrium (initial SM of 1550, UZ of 40) to see how much the NSE depends on that.

The fit has stabilized at an NSE of 0.228, which is more stationary. Next I'll recalibrate the model from an equilibrium start, though every change to the FC value shifts that equilibrium again. I'm also weighing whether to try the KGE or revisit the model's structure. On the soil side, the large FC and the BETA of 1.19 suggest it acts as a multi-year memory store, while the upper and lower stores contribute only small outflows.

I'm thinking about the lower store's sink coefficient K2, which at its current value contributes a trend of about 15% of mean flow by the end of the record. That dependence on the starting storage could skew the 1998–2008 evaluation. I'm considering widening the parameter range down toward zero so the lower store acts as a pure sink, and then recalibrating with DDS for 1500 iterations from the current point. I'm also wondering whether to allow FC above 5000, even though 2829 already looks physically implausible.

input.diagnosis: Performance is poor. Daily NSE is about 0.28–0.30 over 1971–1997 (KGE about 0.57, r about 0.59, bias within ±7%). The Wandle is a chalk-fed, heavily urbanised catchment. Observed runoff is only about 0.13 mm/day, roughly 6% of rainfall, and the hydrograph is strongly damped (peak about 1.6 mm/day). Most recharge evidently leaves the catchment through inter-catchment groundwater flow or abstraction. Standard HBV cannot lose water, so I made the lower store a pure sink (K2 = 0). PERC (about 1.07 mm/day) therefore acts as a loss. The upper store, which drains very slowly (K1 about 0.0017/day), plays the chalk aquifer, and a very large soil store (FC about 5000 mm, LP 0.97) adds memory from one year to the next. These values are not physically meaningful; they are tricks that make the model behave like the catchment. Weaknesses: the model misses the timing of seasonal and drought recovery (correlation is only about 0.6), misses short urban storm peaks, and does not simulate the 1976 and 1990–92 droughts well. Starting stores are set near equilibrium for late 1997 (soil about 3070 mm, upper store 64 mm). Because the soil store is so large, the result depends strongly on these starting values: default starting states would give far too little flow for several years. Confidence in individual parameters is low because several are strongly interdependent. Expected NSE in 1998–2008 is about 0.2–0.3.
